---
title: "Introduction"
numbered: true
bibliography: refs/thesis.bib
---

Although education has been a fundamental pillar of society because it promotes equal opportunities and social mobility, significant inequalities still persist within the education system. For example, [@blanden_educational_2022] state that, in countries with greater inequality, educational gaps perpetuate inequalities of origin: “If higher inequality increases the gap in educational achievements between children from richer and poorer families, lower social mobility is likely to follow” (pp. 2). Inequalities have also been found across various dimensions within education, such as gender, race, and intergenerational educational attainment, to name a few [@quinn_politics_2017; @oecd_education_2025]. However, one of the most troubling issues in recent years has been the commodification of education, as private alternatives have emerged worldwide to compete with public institutions, which has had consequences not only at the institutional level but also at the cultural level [@busemeyer_welfare_2020; @busemeyer_investing_2018]. Along these lines, a research agenda has been developed focusing on attitudes toward inequality in education [@busemeyer_education_2013; @castillo_changes_2025; @lindh_public_2015].

Although one might expect most people to support public education—especially in countries with greater inequality—various studies have shown that some segments of the population support the private alternative and may even justify the inequalities it creates [@lindh_public_2015]. This runs counter to the principles of equality that underpin social justice and, in particular, educational justice [@moyano_justicia_2020; @walzer_spheres_2010; @deutsch_equity_1975]. The concept of “market justice” is fundamental to understanding this phenomenon; the term proposed by @lane_market_1986 refers to the normative beliefs that legitimize the idea that access to essential social goods—such as education—should be governed by market criteria [@lindh_public_2015]. This research will draw on the concept of market justice in education to examine the extent to which people legitimize inequality in this sphere.

In the context of legitimizing inequalities, meritocracy has been presented as one of the most important explanatory factors [@clycq_meritocracy_2014; @heuer_legitimizing_2020; @morris_paradox_2022; @mijs_paradox_2021]. Known as a distributive system based on effort and talent [@young_rise_2017], a meritocratic narrative has been constructed that attributes responsibility for success or failure to the individual. In this way, the role that structural conditions play in individuals’ life trajectories is overlooked, serving as a mechanism for justifying inequalities [@mijs_unfulfillable_2016]. With regard to market justice, it has been observed that meritocratic beliefs are positively associated with it, especially with the perception of meritocracy [@castillo_socialization_2024; @castillo_perceptions_2025; @castillo_justification_2026]. That said, researchers have made progress in deepening our understanding of meritocracy, going so far as to outline multidimensional frameworks. For example, @castillo_multidimensional_2023 proposed a conceptual framework that distinguishes between perceptions and preferences regarding meritocratic aspects and those related to privilege. Although these concepts may sound contradictory, there is evidence suggesting that they are distinct constructs and can therefore coexist [@castillo_multidimensional_2023; @mijs_inequality_2018]. Thus, while it is known that there are different dimensions of meritocracy, it remains unclear which beliefs predominate among the general population.

Researchers have shown that, based on a set of beliefs (such as those offered by the @castillo_multidimensional_2023 multidimensional framework), these beliefs are organized and predominate differently in people’s minds. This can be understood as a belief system, and a belief system can be representative of a social group with common characteristics; however, to observe this, it is necessary to use person-centered methods, which are rare in sociology [@zhu_meritocratic_2025; @vanhootegem_worlds_2022]. Methods such as Latent Class Analysis (LCA) allow us to observe the heterogeneity of beliefs by classifying subgroups, as well as their prevalence in terms of number and size [@collins_latent_2013; @scottorosato_latent_2012]. Thus, the formation of different subgroups based on meritocratic beliefs could subsequently provide new insights into the relationship between meritocracy and market justice in education. Based on this, the questions this research seeks to answer are:  (1) How do meritocratic belief systems manifest in terms of the number of identifiable groups and their sizes? (2) To what extent do meritocratic belief systems influence preferences for market-based justice in education?

This research contributes to the agenda of meritocracy and market justice through two innovations: First, it explores meritocratic belief systems using a multidimensional framework that distinguishes between what people observe (perceptions) and their normative orientation (preferences) regarding both merit and privilege. Second, it analyzes the relationship between different meritocratic belief systems and market justice in education. The argument underpinning these objectives is that, in belief systems where merit-based beliefs predominate, their relationship with market justice in education will be positive, reinforcing the narrative of meritocracy as a legitimizer of inequalities. Furthermore, drawing on the various relationships between meritocratic belief systems and market justice in education, it aims to demonstrate that meritocracy can function in different ways as a mechanism for justifying inequalities, but this can only be observed by examining the diversity of people’s beliefs as belief systems.

This study is particularly relevant in Chile, a country characterized by high levels of inequality and a system in which social goods are highly commodified [@boccardo_30_2020; @castillo_changes_2025]. The neoliberal reforms of the civil-military dictatorship (1973–1989) have produced structurally segmented systems in health care, pensions, and education, in which access and quality depend on ability to pay, benefiting higher-income sectors and relegating the poorest to limited, underfunded public alternatives [@madariaga_three_2020]. Specifically, the education system is highlighted as one of the most privatized in the world, where the quality of private education surpasses that of public education due to limited regulation of the education market, as reflected in high levels of school segregation and low regard for public education [@bellei_problema_2025; @bellei_gran_2016; @ramos_educacion_2022; @valenzuela_socioeconomic_2014]. Despite this, people continue to hold strong meritocratic beliefs, illustrating the inequality paradox [@pnud_desiguales_2017; @mijs_paradox_2021]. Thus, in a context marked by high and durable inequalities, deep marketization of education, and the entrenchment of meritocratic beliefs, it is relevant to examine the link between meritocratic beliefs and market-justice preferences in education.
